projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with George Yaworski was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the Oral History of World War II Veteran George Yaworski. Mr. Yaworski served in the US Coast Guard on board the USS Aquarius AKA 16. He served in the pacific theater and his highest rank was third class cook. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Yaworski home in metro Ohio on December 13th 2004. George was 81 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I was living in Pennsylvania, Freeland, Pennsylvania but I was in a CCC camps out in Montana and when the war broke out they had us sign up at the Libby, Montana draft board so we signed up and then when they disbanded the CCC camps they sent me back to Freeland, Pennsylvania. I wanted to join the Coast Guard so I had to write to Libby, Montana to get a release to get permission to join the Coast Guard.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of work were you doing with the CCC?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I was a cook for the camp. I cooked for 200 men.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Nothing in particular stands out?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: They just said that war broke out nobody believed it they just like everybody else. You don't believe we're at war with Japan or Germany.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't necessarily believe you were going to be _____with them?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No, but when I got home I hitch hiked down to Philadelphia that was their mode of transportation back then. And then about 5 doctors examined me and they found me fit for duty for the Merchant Marine but I was under age and my older brother was in the Coast Guard told my mother not to sign the papers because she would never see me again. So instead of joining the Merchant Marine I joined the Coast Guard. And I took boot camp in Manhattan Beach and they sent me up to Groden, Connecticut permanent detail and I didn't want permanent detail everybody was going oversees but me. So about 5 of us went to the Chaplin and griped because we weren't going oversees he just said relax and everything will work out so I asked one of the other guys at the Groden Coast Guard station how would I get out of here? he said, "Well you got to go to school." so I picked cooks and bakers school and after I graduated they sent me out to a Coast Guard station in Manistee, Michigan that had their accommodations for 12 men and I was suppose to cook for men who had ships blown up under them in North Atlantic so we had as high as 36 men at the Manistee station. So they ate in shifts, 12 guys at each shift. So after several years they told me to pick up the Aquarius in San Pedro.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you go into the Navy then?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: In 42

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In 42. So what was it about 44 or so about

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea, they told me to go out to San Pedro and get on the Aquarius. So I took an I think it was train out to San Pedro and got on the Aquarius and that's it. The war

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why don't you describe what kind of ship that is?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: It's a, it's a like a Liberty Ship and--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It's armed too, right?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea, They had guns on it, but when we come back from China they took the guns off and then we went down around through the Panama Canal and up the Hampton Rose, Virginia and then to Lumper I believe it says in there and then we went up to Sheephead Bay, where they lay the ship up and since I was a cook I was one of the last guys off the ship they discharged everybody but me and finally I got released.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you go to sea then? In 44 was it late 44 probably

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea in the pacific. Yea and the war ended in 45 and we hauled Chinese troops Chiang Kai-shek troops from Hong Kong to Sing Town(ph) and Ching Wang Town(ph) and we had a chinese cook on there and his parents lived in Sing Town(ph) and he swore that if he had enough time he would go over to see them. I don't know if he ever went over there. But we originally hauled airplane parts to Guam. And then we went and picked up the Second Marine Division took them to Nagasaki and then the war ended and we hauled Chinese troops.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you participate in any landings operations?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No No, the war ended before the first tour that the Aquarius had I think she won several battle stars; it's inside the cover there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it looks like here in this scrapbook July 19th of 44.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You reported to board in San Francisco is when you got on the Aquarius?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And July 20th departed San Francisco, arrive San Diego for amphibious maneuvers, what can you tell me about that?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Well we just sailed up and down the west coast and then all I remember is every Sunday the old man said air your bedding and we had to take our mattresses out and hang um over the side of ship and then after Sunday they brought them back in and you made your bed and that was it

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughing)

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Some of the guys lost their mattresses so I don't know what they did if they had new ones issued or if they just had to sleep on the springs, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was life at sea like?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: It was interesting after we picked up the Marines, the Second Division, we had Marines in our quarters and there's one guy on the bottom bunk opposite me he spent all day just spitting and shining his shoes. He had a big handlebar moustache and no matter when you come in he would be there polishing and spitting on his shoes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughing)

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: And then for every 20 Marines that we picked up they gave us a Marine cook well they were pretty nice in the beginning and then they started getting frisky they'd we wore t-shirts and they'd pick up an egg and put it under your t-shirt and break it. And I told them don't fool with me I had lifted weights at the time and this young Marine come up and put and egg up my t-shirt and smashed it and I chased him around the galley and when I got him I ripped his pocket seam half way down his leg and he was mad at first but then we got to be good friends. When he, before he got off the ship he gave me a pair of Marine shoes, they wore like iron. I had them for several years after I got out. That was about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So I'm guessing these dates here are July of 1945

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So I think it said 44 so I think July 45 is when you first reported. Let's see then your first oversees trip then was to Guam in September, September 4th that is when you took the airplane parts.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uneventful?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Nope, we zig zaged over across the pacific and every time the old man saw a flying fish he'd stop the ship and fish awhile and if he didn't get anything he'd start her up and we'd be on our way again.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you took that trip it looks like between the time that they had dropped the bomb and before the peace treaty was signed so was there still fear there would be some hostile action?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea. We thought we were going to get into some action, but it didn't work out that way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news about the atomic bombs?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Well they had a newspaper on aboard ship and they they had the report in the newspaper.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any particular celebrations were there in the news?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Naw, I guess I was in the galley and you know usually the celebrations are out on deck or in different departments so I didn't see any of that stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I--the question just slipped my mind. Oh I know what I'd like to ask you about I assume you probably went through the ceremony where you crossed the equator?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about that?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: It wasn't much. I guess we on the way over we missed the Tuesday and then on the way back we got two Thursdays in our schedule and that's about all I remember crossing the equator.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't have to go through that little shellback and all that stuff

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No. I didn't have to

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughing) so did you get a chance; you took marines, the Second Marine Division to Nagasaki

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Nagasaki, did you get a chance to go a shore there at all.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I went a shore but I was wearing my cooks clothes and I didn't have my ID with me, so I went a shore because this Marine Guard he made several trips back and forth and I went a shore and I just went up into the mountains and when I cam back down they didn't want to let me back on the boat because I didn't have my ID with me. But I talked them into it and I got back onboard ship and I remember don't ever leave the ship without your ID.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you see any of the demonstrations in the city?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Oh yea. We saw where they had the one man submarines, where they built them all the overhead iron bars were all twisted and bent out of shape.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: We're they warning you to stay away from where the bomb had actually hit?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No, they didn't

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There was no fear about radiation or anything like that at that time.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No. They never know anything about radiation at that time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Didn't know enough about it

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Right, Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Obviously you had no after effects from being near it, right?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No. I didn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else you can tell me about Nagasaki?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Not much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Next you went to the Philippines in October, October 1st arrived in Nineveh(sp)

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea and then they had these sketch artists that would draw your picture for a buck and stuff like that and the jewelers instead of having a jewelry store that you walked into he had a couple of cantaloupe crates and he had all of his watches displayed in there so you could go by and pick up a watch or whatever you wanted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there much souvenir collecting going on as you stopped at these places?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: They had bum boats that came around the stern of the ship and they had long poles and they had a little basket on it so you'd take a cigarette lighter or whatever packet of cigarettes and drop it in and they would lower it and pick up whatever you gave them and then they would send up a watch or something, whatever.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So there wasn't a lot of collecting of military souvenirs and things like that?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was the Philippines like? Did you go a shore in Manila?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea. There's pictures in that book there about --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: One if the few monuments that defined Manila was devastated right?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did the guys in the pacific think of Macarthur?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: They never talked much about him

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just didn't. Yea.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Like I say in the galley you you don't discuss Generals.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many guys were in the galley working with you?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: About a dozen I guess. And we worked 2 days on and 2 days off. So you're out in the pacific and you have 2 days off what are you going to do? So you go out on deck and you watch the Marines go through their training and their using one of the boats that took us to shore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So that was kind of how you were able to pass the time watch them training. Any other entertainment or do anything to amuse yourself?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Well, they had movies at night. But old movies we probably saw them several times already. But whatever they showed you, that's what you either went to the movies or go to your room.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't think I've asked a cook this before, but what was the food like in the Navy?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: It wasn't bad, it was alright. When we got supplies they sent me down to the first platform below the galley and they said make sure everything coming aboard goes right to the galley while they had some big 6 foot tall engineer standing there and a case of oranges come up and he opened the door and they went into the engine room I wasn't about to tell him that that stuff belonged to the galley. I wouldn't argue with a big 6 footer, not me. But the engine room and the galley were good friends they used to make ice for us and we made ice cream and gave it to them and everybody was happy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How about mail call? Did you get much in the way of packages and letters?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Well my girlfriend at the time she sent me quite a few letters. But I'd write everyday and I'd number the letter on the back so when she got em she could put them in proper order. Because you didn't get mail too often. And then when we got to Guam my brother was on Tamuning Island and you could see Tamuning from Guam so, so I used one of these crank telephones that you crank up and I tried to call my brother and I couldn't get a response so I went back to my room and wrote a letter and they sent it to San Francisco and then San Francisco sent it back to Tamuning and he found out that our ship was in the bay and he got on one of the garbage boats that collects garbage from all the ships and I guess it took him 4 hours to get to our ship and when he got there he came on board and he ate supper with me and then the next morning the captain took him back to the shore in his little whatever you call those little boats

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Dingy

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea, dingy. He got the cutest little dingy in the Navy. (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughing) So how long did it take that letter to get to San Francisco and then back to him?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I don't know

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Obviously it wasn't too long, right?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No it come in maybe about maybe 3 days and we happened to be there so he came on board and we spent the night together

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So I didn't realize that apparently Guam, Tamuning and Taipan were all kind of the same area.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you see all 3 of them basically….?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I don't think you could see 3 of them, I think you could see Tamuning from Guam maybe but not Taipan

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea, I had no idea either. So anything else about Manila that you remember?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No, they had these stage shows where the people walked on rope and stuff but it wasn't much we've seen all that stuff before.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't get any USO shows are anything like that, did you?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then you picked up the Chinese troops. Were they pretty friendly with the Americans?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea, but the old man took all the ammunition away from them -

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Chinese

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: He let them have their guns because you can't stack a lot if guns, ya know, and then but they were okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now why? They were supposedly out allies at the time, correct?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why would he take the ammo away? Just in case?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea, just in case, yea. You never know if somebody is going to go wacko and try something.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A few drinks, whatever.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But there shouldn't be alcohol on the ship right?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Shouldn't of been but when we unloaded in record time the old man gave everybody 2 cartons of cigarettes and a couple cans of 4.0 beer. And then some of the guys took the cigarettes to shore and sold them for seven or eight dollars a carton. I guess they were 55 cents a carton on board ship. And the you weren't allowed to take them on shore and sell them but the guys had bell bottoms so they would just pull up the bell bottoms and tape the carton of cigarettes on their calves and pull their pants down over them you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you didn't have any trouble with the Chinese then on that trip did you?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No, No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever have a chance to talk to any of them?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Well I can't talk chinese.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There were no english speaking Chinese there.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Oh no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So not a lot of communication

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: But we put the steam cookers out on deck and we cooked rice out on deck and then they had rice every meal but every other meal they put some kind of meat in it, chicken or corned beef or beef. And one morning I went out I was gong to fill that biggest steam kettle I was going to fill it up with water and I lifted the cover and there was a chinese soldier curled up in there asleep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughing) I guess he got a little cold during the night or something?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I have no idea. But he was curled up in that steam cooker.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well good thing you didn't turn on the heat first.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea. And some of the steam pipes lead from the galley on to the steam cooker and some of those chinese wander around bare foot and step on that pipe and they would go up air and land on it again and they'd go up again. You had to warn them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies on your crew?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea, I had a couple of close friends. Some guy from San Antonio, Texas we made a bet together, this is when you're young and dumb. I bet him that I could drink half a dozen raw eggs in the morning and a half a dozen raw eggs in the afternoon and they wouldn't bother me and he made the same bet. So when we left China it took us 30 days to come back to the states and we each made sure that we drank our eggs. So I drank a case of eggs from China back to Seattle.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Laughing---

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: And he drank a case of eggs. There's 30 dozen in a case, and it took us 30 days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Nobody won the bet?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You both kept up?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I just had four-way bypass surgery so I don't know if it did me any good or not.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughing) Well you're still here. Let's see November it looks like you went to Okinawa? Did you spend anytime on Okinawa or any of the islands there?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No, No. We just went there and unloaded and took off.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It looks like you were headed back to North America after that, right?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea. That's when I drank all them eggs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughing) You had to have something to pass the time.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Boy, were we a bunch of weirdoes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose anybody on your ship?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How big was that crew?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I think there was a couple of hundred. I don't know. I'm not sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you mentioned there was a burial at sea for one of the chinese soldiers.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How would you describe that?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Well, he had, I guess he had diarrhea and they couldn't stop it they tried but he passed on. So then they had a burial at sea. They just took a piece of canvas and laid him on it and put a couple of 5 inch shells along side sewed it up they had a board out on deck and only the officers went to the funeral. The rest of the chinese were in the stern of the ship having a good time and we stood there and we had a salute when he slid the body into the water. That was about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You said the chinese did not consider it to be an honor at all to be buried at sea?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Correct. Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And what would they do when their sailors or whatever died at sea?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I don't know. I don't think they had a navy did they?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't know. You'd think they'd have a gun boat or something.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: and

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They probably didn't have much of a Navy, come to think of it

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, they were at war with Japan for many years before we got into it to.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No not really. Well before we left Seattle one of the fellows who was waiting tables in the officer's mess stabbed another guy to death. They got into an argument and he threw the gun, the knife over the side so when they had the trial they didn't have any evidence so I don't know what the result was. I don't know if he was freed or if he went to jail or whatever it was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were there any witnesses?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Only, the only witnesses were the guy after he got through stabbing him, he come out on deck and I think a Bosen Mate grabbed him and took him to to the jail wherever that was below deck.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So no one saw the actual stabbing and they didn't have the knife

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Probably didn't get convicted of something.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: And we didn't in the galley we didn't have any sifter for the flour and the flour had bugs in it so we just baked the bugs right in in the bread. And at meal time you could see the guys pick up a slice of bread and hold it up to the light and put all the bugs on one place and they'd eat the bread then they'd take and scrape up all the bugs and throw them in a --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh man. (laughing)

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Poke them out of there?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And there's a picture here, you talked about this before we started rolling the tape here picture here of the toilet facilities that you had to use for a while?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Just the chinese.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The chinese, okay.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now why did they have to—it's a picture here of them going to the bathroom or an area were they went to the bathroom at the stern of the ship, right?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Right. It was just a big trough. Water came in the forward end and just washed everything off over the sten.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that because there weren't enough facilities for them?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Oh no. They had communicable disease and they didn't want them in our bathrooms.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yea and you said they had some nurses along? Tell that again?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: They had nurses and every time a nurse would go out to go to the bathroom half the crew went out to watch them so the Captain had the carpenters built a couple of shacks over top some of the holes

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And at least one of the soldiers here had a baby, right?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yes, well all some of those soldiers were 11, 12 years old and they kept their chopsticks inside their leggings and each one had a little like a sock full of rice that they wore around their neck and I guess if they invited you to eat some of their rice then it was suppose to be a big honor for you. It was an honor for you to eat their rice.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did the guys like having a baby on board ship?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Well they didn't get to bother, it's just---

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Didn't bother? Anything else that comes to mind?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: No, not really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Alright, very good. That's right you spent a short time on the SS Fitzgerald, right?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Oh yea, right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long were you on that ship?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: I was on for 73 and 74 she sank in 75.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How soon after you left the ship did it sink? About a year or so?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. What was that ship like?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Its 729 feet long. It was a beautiful ship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Probably a lot bigger than the ship you were on before?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea. It was built in 1958 nobody ever thought it would go down.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you know any of the guys who went down with the ship?

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Just about all of them

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. It says the AKA is actually an attack cargo ship.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Yea. The APAs were personnel assaults they just had people on them but the AKAs we had Marines, we had their ducks, their swimmers whatever their boats and I used to exercise with weights and then when we brought the Marines on board one of the Marines took all of the weights and hid them in a jeep so I got the guy who was in charge of that group and I took all the weights back again and hid them and when he got that jeep on Guam or wherever it was that we dropped him off he probably tore that Jeep apart and he couldn't find any weights.

sp.speaker: George Yaworski
sp.p: Laughing During this interview I mistakenly said a couple of times that George was in the Navy, he was in the Coast Guard. Thank you.
